hooks.text: Dead stars are supposed to destroy worlds, not build new ones.
A dead star is actively cannibalizing a planet made from its ashes.
Can a dead star actually build a brand new solar system?

title: How Dead Stars Can Spawn New Planets
description: Archival Hubble and TESS data show a dead white dwarf star stripping the atmosphere of a second-generation planet born from its own ruins.

beats.text: Dead stars are supposed to destroy worlds, not build new ones.
beats.visual: artist concept of an exoplanet orbiting a white dwarf 2021

beats.text: Most astronomers believed a white dwarf, the dense remnant core of a dead star, was a planetary graveyard.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope image of the Ring Nebula 2013

beats.text: But in 1999, Hubble spotted mystery chemical signatures around a distant white dwarf.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope in orbit over Earth 2009

beats.text: Recently, researcher Jamie Williams used new data to solve this cosmic cold case.
beats.visual: photograph of the University of Warwick campus 2018

beats.text: The mystery signatures turned out to be niobium, a heavy metal forged only during stellar death throes.
beats.visual: illustration of stellar nucleosynthesis inside a dying star

beats.text: NASA's TESS telescope then detected a Jupiter-sized candidate planet orbiting the dead star every 4.4 days.
beats.visual: artist concept of TESS spacecraft in space 2018

beats.text: The white dwarf's intense radiation is stripping this second-generation planet's atmosphere, raining those heavy metals back down.
beats.visual: artist concept of an evaporating hot Jupiter exoplanet 2015

beats.text: This cosmic recycling shows why dead stars are actually building new ones.
beats.visual: artist concept of a white dwarf accreting debris 2020
